entries.topicDescription: Modern async/await and task-based concurrency in Swift.

tips.title: async/await replaces completion handlers
tips.content:
Swift's async/await lets you write asynchronous code that
reads like synchronous code. Mark a function 'async' and
call it with 'await' — no more callback pyramids.

The compiler suspends execution at each 'await' point and
resumes when the result is ready. Errors propagate naturally
with try/catch instead of Result types in callbacks.

Async functions can only be called from other async contexts:
other async functions, Task blocks, or async main entry points.

This model eliminates common callback bugs: forgetting to call
the completion handler, calling it twice, or calling it on the
wrong thread.

tips.title: TaskGroup runs concurrent work with structured lifetimes
tips.content:
When you need to run multiple async operations concurrently,
use 'withTaskGroup'. It creates child tasks that run in
parallel but are scoped to the group.

Structured concurrency guarantees: if the group scope ends,
all child tasks are cancelled. If a child throws, the group
can cancel siblings. No orphaned tasks.

Use 'withThrowingTaskGroup' when child tasks can throw errors.
Collect results by iterating over the group — each value
arrives as its task completes.

This replaces DispatchGroup and manual synchronization with
a safe, compiler-checked model.

tips.title: Actors protect mutable state from data races
tips.content:
An actor is a reference type that protects its mutable state
by serializing access. Only one task can execute an actor's
methods at a time — the compiler enforces this.

Accessing an actor's properties or methods from outside
requires 'await', because the call may need to wait for
exclusive access. Inside the actor, access is synchronous.

The @MainActor attribute marks code that must run on the main
thread. SwiftUI views and UIKit updates use this to guarantee
UI work happens on the correct thread.

Actors replace manual locks, serial queues, and other
synchronization primitives with a safe, language-level model.
